--name=ite
--context_item_type=def
/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

  toFun := (fun t : ℝ => if t ≤ 1 / 2 then γ.extend (2 * t) else γ'.extend (2 * t - 1)) ∘ (↑)

    refine

        continuous_subtype_val <;>
    fun_prop

  target' := by norm_num

--name=ite

/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)

--name=ite
--context_item_type=def
/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.

/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/

/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)

--name=ite
--context_item_type=def
/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

def trans (γ : Path x y) (γ' : Path y z) : Path x z where
  toFun := (fun t : ℝ => if t ≤ 1 / 2 then γ.extend (2 * t) else γ'.extend (2 * t - 1)) ∘ (↑)
  continuous_toFun := by
    refine
      (Continuous.if_le ?_ ?_ continuous_id continuous_const (by norm_num)).comp
        continuous_subtype_val <;>
    fun_prop
  source' := by norm_num
  target' := by norm_num

--name=ite
--context_item_type=def
/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

/-- Concatenation of two paths from `x` to `y` and from `y` to `z`, putting the first
path on `[0, 1/2]` and the second one on `[1/2, 1]`. -/
@[trans]
def trans (γ : Path x y) (γ' : Path y z) : Path x z where
  toFun := (fun t : ℝ => if t ≤ 1 / 2 then γ.extend (2 * t) else γ'.extend (2 * t - 1)) ∘ (↑)
  continuous_toFun := by
    refine
      (Continuous.if_le ?_ ?_ continuous_id continuous_const (by norm_num)).comp
        continuous_subtype_val <;>
    fun_prop
  source' := by norm_num
  target' := by norm_num

/--

return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/

  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)

--name=ite

/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.

`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and

until `c` is known.

/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
</ITEM>

`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.

/--
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
-/
/-
Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
`@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
until `c` is known.
-/
@[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
  h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)

theorem contSupp_supports {S k} (H : contSupp k ⊆ S) : Supports (contSupp k) S := by
  induction k with
  | halt => simp [contSupp_halt, Supports]
  | cons₁ f k IH =>
    have H₁ := H; rw [contSupp_cons₁] at H₁; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H₁
    refine trStmts₁_supports' (trNormal_supports H₂) H₁ fun h => ?_
    refine supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H₂, ?_⟩
    simp only [codeSupp, contSupp_cons₂, Finset.union_subset_iff] at H₂
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports H₂.2.2) (Finset.union_subset_right h) IH
  | cons₂ k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH
  | comp f k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_comp] at H'; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H'
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H', IH H₂⟩
  | fix f k IH =>
    rw [contSupp] at H
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H, IH (Finset.union_subset_right H)⟩

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/

--name=id

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a
</ITEM>

    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH

theorem contSupp_supports {S k} (H : contSupp k ⊆ S) : Supports (contSupp k) S := by
  induction k with
  | halt => simp [contSupp_halt, Supports]
  | cons₁ f k IH =>
    have H₁ := H; rw [contSupp_cons₁] at H₁; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H₁
    refine trStmts₁_supports' (trNormal_supports H₂) H₁ fun h => ?_
    refine supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H₂, ?_⟩
    simp only [codeSupp, contSupp_cons₂, Finset.union_subset_iff] at H₂
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports H₂.2.2) (Finset.union_subset_right h) IH
  | cons₂ k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH
  | comp f k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_comp] at H'; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H'
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H', IH H₂⟩
  | fix f k IH =>
    rw [contSupp] at H
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H, IH (Finset.union_subset_right H)⟩

(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,

knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.

  induction k with

  | cons₁ f k IH =>

    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports H₂.2.2) (Finset.union_subset_right h) IH
  | cons₂ k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH

    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_comp] at H'; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H'

The goal is to prove that for continuous functors, the transitive closure ofConditions is transitive. The step function transweekly helps in this proof by property composition and idempotent closure.

We use properties of continuous functors, specifically the `isClosed` property, to show that the composition of the transitive closure with itself equals the transitive closure itself, hence proving it is idempotent. Additionally, using `Subtype.ext` and `trans weekly` properties, we show that the composition of transitions is transitive culminating in the desired result.

--name=id
--context_item_type=def
/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,

theorem contSupp_supports {S k} (H : contSupp k ⊆ S) : Supports (contSupp k) S := by
  induction k with
  | halt => simp [contSupp_halt, Supports]
  | cons₁ f k IH =>
    have H₁ := H; rw [contSupp_cons₁] at H₁; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H₁
    refine trStmts₁_supports' (trNormal_supports H₂) H₁ fun h => ?_
    refine supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H₂, ?_⟩
    simp only [codeSupp, contSupp_cons₂, Finset.union_subset_iff] at H₂
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports H₂.2.2) (Finset.union_subset_right h) IH
  | cons₂ k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH
  | comp f k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_comp] at H'; have H₂ := Finset.union_subset_right H'
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H', IH H₂⟩
  | fix f k IH =>
    rw [contSupp] at H
    exact supports_union.2 ⟨codeSupp'_supports H, IH (Finset.union_subset_right H)⟩

(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.

 nag by using reparametrization, I decomposed the concatenated paths into their constituent segments and compared their parametrizations. I then used the properties of continuous functions and homotopy to show that each segment of the first path is homotopic to the corresponding segment of the second path, and hence the entire paths are homotopic and therefore identical as closed paths. function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,

typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`

(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`

--name=id
--context_item_type=def
/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

--name=id
--context_item_type=def
/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a
</ITEM>

  | cons₂ k IH =>
    have H' := H; rw [contSupp_cons₂] at H'
    exact trStmts₁_supports' (head_supports <| Finset.union_subset_right H') H' IH

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,

knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.
